newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: N.Korean breakthrough with Cargill is barter deal.
newsitem.headline: N.Korean breakthrough with Cargill is barter deal.

text.p: In a breakthrough barter deal, U.S. grains giant Cargill Inc will make probably the first direct American grain sale to hunger-stricken North Korea since the 1950-53 Korean War, traders in Seoul said on Tuesday.
They said Cargill would swap 20,000 tonnes of wheat for 4,000 tonnes of zinc, with each commodity worth $4 million.

Cargill spokeswoman Lori Johnson, unveiling the hard-fought agreement on Monday, said only that the company would sell an unspecified amount of wheat. She added the deal might signal further sales of U.S. grain to Pyongyang.
On Tuesday, a U.N. official in Geneva said North Korea had told international aid agencies 134 children had died of malnutrition.
It was believed to be the first time North Korea has publicly acknowledged its people were dying as a result of chronic food shortages.
Pyongyang has been demanding food aid in return for an agreement to take part in peace talks proposed by the United States and South Korea.
The talks, also including China, are aimed at securing a peace treaty to replace a truce that ended the Korean War.
Separately, religious and other civic groups in South Korea said on Tuesday they planned to raise about $20 million to ship 110,000 tonnes of corn to hunger-stricken North Korea.
This comes on top of a World Food Programme (WFP) appeal for 200,000 tonnes of food aid.
Together, these supplies would amount to 330,000 tonnes, making up for 14 percent of North Korea's food shortage of 2.3 million tonnes this year, according to WFP estimates.
Seoul officials said North Korea was pushing for membership of the Asian Development Bank, which would make it eligible for soft loans.
The Cargill deal was struck in Beijing last Saturday, the Seoul traders close to the transaction said.
The wheat shipment was expected to leave the United States in early May and arrive in North Korea later in the month, while the zinc would be shipped in two cargoes in May and June.
Earlier, U.S. officials said it was probably the first direct sale of U.S. grown wheat to North Korea since the Korean War, when Washington imposed a tight ban on trade with Pyongyang.
Cargill and North Korea have been discussing the wheat sale since January following approval by the U.S. government to sell 500,000 tonnes of wheat and/or rice to the communist country.

In Vietnam on Tuesday, North Korea's deputy premier Kong Jin-tae, the most senior Pyongyang official to visit the southeast Asian nation in several years, held talks with Hanoi officials to try to hammer out grain deals.

An official with Vietnam's state Southern Food Corporation told Reuters that Kong was expected to seek an undisclosed increase in imports of rice from Vietnam, which in 1996 were variously put between 20,000 and 40,000 tonnes.

In Seoul, six religious groups and 22 civic organisations said they had raised raised 1.37 billion won ($1.53 million) and set a target of raising 17 billion won ($18.99 million) over the next two months to provide corn to the North.
Last week, the South Korean Red Cross sent more than $1 million worth of food and vegetable seed to North Korea, its largest delivery since such shipments began in November 1995.
Also last week, the Seoul government lifted a ban on private organisations providing rice to Pyongyang and allowed local business groups to join food aid programmes for the North.
